title: Workshop overview
content:
Introduction CloudDocs is an enterprise document management system that has been developed and integrated with AWS services. The project uses Amazon EC2 for the application environment, Amazon RDS MySQL for business data, Amazon S3 for private document storage and Amazon Cognito for user authentication.
This workshop presents the architecture, configuration steps and practical results of the system. Screenshots in the following sections illustrate AWS settings and functions exercised in CloudDocs.
Workshop objectives Understand the roles and relationships of EC2, RDS MySQL, S3, Cognito and IAM in the system. Understand environment configuration, service connections and application deployment. Explain sign-in, upload, preview, download and document authorization flows. Compare practical results using AWS configuration, application screens and activity logs. Architecture overview The HTML, CSS and JavaScript frontend communicates with the Spring Boot backend through REST APIs. The backend connects to RDS MySQL for metadata and business data, verifies identities issued by Cognito and receives multipart requests to upload files to S3. For preview/download, it issues presigned GET URLs for direct browser access to S3. An IAM role and bucket policy authorize cross-account S3 access as shown in the diagram.
Main processing flows The user signs in through Cognito using Authorization Code + PKCE; the frontend receives an access token. The frontend sends REST API requests with a Bearer token; the backend validates the JWT and checks the account and role in MySQL. The frontend sends POST /api/documents/upload as multipart with file, metadata, requestId and optional folderId. The backend checks the quota and folder scope before completing the transaction. The backend stores the file in S3, checks it with HeadObject and commits metadata only after success. Retrying the same account-scoped requestId returns the saved document if compatible; on failure, data is rolled back and cleanup of the upload attempt’s object is attempted. For preview or download, the backend checks current permissions and issues a time-limited presigned GET URL. Sharing, trash, restore, task assignment and report review are handled by the backend; business records and activity logs are stored in MySQL. Completed functionality The system includes sign-in and sign-out, document management, upload, preview, download, search, permission-based sharing, favorites, trash and restore. User management, storage statistics, activity logs, notifications and the task assignment – report submission – approval workflow have also been added to the application.
The current source also contains the following functions; existing practice screenshots do not illustrate every new function:
Group Functions in the current source Department authorization ADMIN/MANAGER/USER; MANAGER previews documents owned by accounts in the same department and assigns work to USER accounts in that department Folders Create subfolders, rename and move one/multiple files; moving preserves S3 keys, shares and favorites Sharing and content Sent shares supports changing/revoking permissions; content replacement preserves document IDs and existing relationships Profiles and administration Manage departments, assign staff, update profiles and avatars Interface Pagination of 20 items on main lists, search/filter/sort and browser history navigation Pagination currently operates on data already loaded in the browser rather than database queries. Backend upload avoids completing metadata before a file is stored, but requires appropriate multipart limits in Nginx and the backend. Failed object cleanup requires log reconciliation because S3 and MySQL have no distributed transaction.
Practical illustrations of these functions appear in 4.8. Business and integration testing. The configuration sections below combine procedural guidance with screenshots from the practice environment so that readers can compare each architecture component.

title: Proposal
content:
This section presents CloudDocs — Enterprise document management on the AWS cloud.
CloudDocs — Enterprise document management on AWS A solution combining Spring Boot, MySQL, S3 and Cognito 1. Executive summary CloudDocs centralizes documents and work-processing workflows in a web application. ADMIN administers the system; MANAGER monitors documents and assigns work within their department; USER manages owned or shared documents and performs assigned tasks. Java 21/Spring Boot 3.5.6 provides REST APIs and authorization; HTML/CSS/JavaScript provides the frontend; MySQL stores metadata, sharing relationships, quotas and business audit records. Files are stored in private S3, with authentication through a Cognito User Pool.
The target architecture uses EC2 for the application and Nginx, RDS MySQL for the database and an IAM role for S3 access. The application uses S3 for documents, Cognito for authentication and MySQL for business data.
2. Problem statement Current problems
Documents scattered across personal devices or chat channels are difficult to find, authorize and trace to the person who changed them. Accidental deletion, excessive sharing, missing capacity controls and disconnected assignments and reports reduce traceability.
Solution
CloudDocs organizes documents by metadata, department and folder hierarchy and supports search/filtering, preview, download, permission-based sharing, favorites and trash. New uploads and content replacements pass through the backend for authorization, quota checks and S3 storage; preview/download use presigned GET URLs issued after authorization. MySQL stores business data and audit records. The current release includes assignments, report submission, approval/change requests, department management and a Sent shares page for changing/revoking permissions.
Benefits and return on investment (ROI)
Reduce manual searching and sharing; measure the time required for the same scenario before and after adoption. Separate file contents from metadata for clearer data management; direct S3 preview/download reduces backend file transfer for read operations. Use trash and audit records to handle mistakes; apply account quotas to control allocations. Financial ROI and savings rates have not been measured. Costs are modeled from assumptions and compared with Billing during deployment. 3. Solution architecture AWS services used or planned for operation
Category Component Role and status Compute Amazon EC2, Nginx Application server environment; EC2 connectivity has been established Database Amazon RDS for MySQL Metadata, users, permissions and audit; RDS MySQL connectivity has been established Storage Amazon S3 Private bucket; backend upload/object confirmation and presigned GET for preview/download; integrated in the code Identity Amazon Cognito User Pool PKCE sign-in and access token issuance; integrated in the code Security/network IAM Role, VPC, Security Group Resource permissions and network restrictions configured per environment Operations CloudWatch, Budgets Resource monitoring, log collection and budget tracking Component design
Frontend: static web interface; the Cognito public client has no client secret. Configure callback, logout and API_BASE for each environment. Backend: validate JWTs, read current roles/status from MySQL, check owner_id and document permissions, and manage upload state and quotas. RDS/MySQL: store users, documents, permissions, favorites, notifications, audit, work_tasks, departments, avatars and document_folders according to the current schema. S3: separate object keys for each upload attempt; original names remain in metadata. Workflow: multipart → backend authorization/quota checks → S3 upload and confirmation → metadata commit; presigned GET is issued after authorization. Account-scoped requestId supports retrying a lost response without duplicating a previously successful upload. On transaction failure, the application rolls back data and attempts object cleanup; S3/MySQL have no distributed transaction, so logs must still be checked for leftover objects. Cognito: link identities by issuer/sub rather than email; distinguish ADMIN/MANAGER/USER system roles from ownership and VIEW/DOWNLOAD/EDIT sharing levels. Legacy local workflow: local file endpoints remain for compatibility. The current frontend uses S3; this does not imply that every historical file has been migrated. Business scope USER MANAGER ADMIN Documents Owned or shared Same as USER, plus preview of documents owned by members of the same department System-wide Assignment Perform assigned tasks Assign to active USER accounts in the same department Assign to active USER/MANAGER accounts Report review No Tasks they assigned Tasks they assigned Account, role and department management No No Yes Department-based preview for MANAGER does not automatically grant download, edit, share or delete permissions. Folders belong to individual accounts; moving files preserves S3 keys, shares and favorites. Content replacement preserves the document ID and existing relationships; report documents are protected according to task status.
4. Technical implementation Implementation stages
Analyze business needs, study AWS and design the permission matrix. Develop the ERD, backend/frontend and metadata APIs; manage source code with Git. Integrate private S3, CORS, presigned URLs, sharing and audit; prepare test cases. Prepare EC2/RDS, the IAM role, Nginx configuration and environment variables. Integrate Cognito and run integration tests; extend quotas, trash, tasks, the MANAGER role, departments and folders. These functions exist in the current source; evidenced results and remaining verification are summarized in section 4.8. Technical requirements
Java 21, Maven, MySQL 8 and Node.js for serving the frontend/testing; the frontend is not React and has no npm build step. A valid base schema and any missing incremental migrations. The application uses ddl-auto=validate and does not create an empty database automatically. AWS account, S3 bucket, Cognito pool/client/domain and RDS endpoint; EC2 and an IAM role when deploying to AWS. Keep passwords, access keys, tokens and client secrets out of the repository. Deployment database connections require TLS; local settings must not be copied unchanged to AWS. 5. Roadmap and milestones Week Period Topic Learning outcome 1 10/08/2026–14/08/2026 AWS accounts, Budgets and Support Understood initial AWS account setup and protection. 2 17/08/2026–21/08/2026 AWS IAM and access management Distinguished users, groups, policies and roles. 3 24/08/2026–28/08/2026 Amazon VPC and network components Understood basic VPC components. 4 31/08/2026–04/09/2026 Amazon EC2 and virtual servers Understood launching and connecting to EC2. 5 07/09/2026–11/09/2026 Managing EC2, EBS and snapshots Distinguished instance lifecycles, EBS volumes, snapshots and AMIs. 6 14/09/2026–18/09/2026 Amazon S3 and AWS CLI Understood the bucket/object model and the AWS CLI’s role. 7 21/09/2026–25/09/2026 S3 security, CORS and presigned URLs Explained private bucket protection and presigned URLs. 8 28/09/2026–02/10/2026 Amazon RDS and MySQL databases Understood RDS MySQL components and connection parameters. 9 05/10/2026–09/10/2026 Amazon RDS backups and security Explained backups, snapshots, restoration and the purpose of Multi-AZ. 10 12/10/2026–16/10/2026 Amazon Cognito and user management Understood User Pools, app clients and sign-in configuration. 11 19/10/2026–23/10/2026 Cognito authentication flows and JWTs Explained Cognito authentication flows and token roles. 12 26/10/2026–30/10/2026 Relationships between AWS services Described an application architecture using the AWS services studied. 6. Budget estimate Demo assumptions: one EC2 instance, one Single-AZ RDS MySQL instance, 5 GB of S3 files, 20 GB of EBS, approximately ten users and 160 infrastructure operating hours per month for learning. These are modeling assumptions, not measured usage or an AWS quotation.
Item Calculation for AWS Pricing Calculator EC2 compute Hourly instance price × 160 hours; compare with 730 hours for continuous operation EBS 20 GB × price per GB-month, including periods when EC2 is stopped RDS compute Hourly DB instance price × actual operating hours RDS storage/backup Allocated capacity × price per GB-month, plus billable backups/snapshots S3 5 GB-month + PUT/GET/HEAD requests + actual data transfer Public IPv4 and networking Number of IPs × billable hours; add NAT Gateway or endpoints if used Cognito Monthly active users and the account’s selected features/tier CloudWatch/Budgets Log volume, retention, metrics/alarms and selected budget features Domain/HTTPS Include only selected services; do not assume Route 53/ALB is used Total Sum all items using the Region, configuration and prices at the estimation date The budget depends on Region, resource configuration, operating time and prices at deployment. Estimates are prepared with AWS Pricing Calculator, while actual usage is tracked through AWS Billing. Storage, snapshots and IP addresses are accounted for separately according to the configuration.
7. Risk assessment Risk matrix
Risk Impact Qualitative likelihood S3 failures caused by incorrect IAM, CORS or Region High Medium RDS connection failure or incorrect schema High Medium Incorrect callback, issuer or app client High Medium Metadata/object inconsistency after failed uploads High Medium Previously issued URLs remain valid after permission revocation Medium A property of the current design Repeated migrations or execution against the wrong database High Medium Charges from retained resources Medium Medium Mitigation strategy
Keep the bucket private, scope the IAM role to the required prefix, authorize requests in the backend and use short-lived URLs. Back up the database, preflight migrations, verify objects with HEAD and test with different accounts. Restrict security groups to permitted sources, use TLS for RDS and keep secrets outside source code. Track costs and clean up demo resources after use.
Contingency plan
Retain the previous build, database backup and controlled environment configuration. If EC2 is unavailable, demonstrate the local application connected to authorized services and identify the demonstration environment accurately. Do not restore a database over active data without a controlled procedure; test restoration on a separate copy first.
8. Expected outcomes Technical improvements
Demonstrate sign-in, upload, preview/download, sharing/revocation and audit; verify ADMIN/MANAGER/USER scopes. Verify quotas, trash, restoration and permanent deletion against metadata/S3. Demonstrate assignments, report submission, pending approval, change requests and late submission in the extended release. Provide deployment instructions, environment configuration and test scenarios matching the actual source code. Check folders, department management, Sent shares and content replacement against the permission matrix; distinguish implemented functions from results verified in practice. Long-term value
Develop skills in backend engineering, authentication, authorization, relational data, object storage and independent architecture research. Possible extensions include automated deployment, improved resilience, file scanning, report versioning and monitoring; count them as completed outcomes only after implementation.
References First Cloud AI Journey AWS Documentation The internship outline and CloudDocs technical documentation.

title: Week 3: Studying Amazon VPC and networking components
content:
Period: 24/08/2026 – 28/08/2026.
This week examines traffic paths in AWS, from address spaces to access controls. The aim is to interpret a basic network diagram for an application with a server and a database.
Weekly objectives Understand the relationship between VPCs, CIDR blocks, subnets and Availability Zones. Distinguish routing from access control using security groups and network ACLs. Learning activities Day Study and review activity Start date Completion date Study sources Monday Study VPCs and CIDR blocks. Review examples of dividing an address space into non-overlapping subnets. 24/08/2026 24/08/2026 Amazon VPC and networking
VPC subnets Tuesday Distinguish public and private subnets through routing configuration. Study how subnets relate to Availability Zones. 25/08/2026 25/08/2026 VPC subnets Wednesday Study route tables, internet gateways and NAT gateways. Analyze outbound Internet paths for different resources. 26/08/2026 26/08/2026 Route tables
NAT gateways Thursday Compare security groups and network ACLs in scope, connection state and rule processing. 27/08/2026 27/08/2026 Security groups
Network ACLs Friday Review a server-and-database network diagram. Identify required connections and paths that should be restricted. 28/08/2026 28/08/2026 Amazon VPC and networking
RDS network and access prerequisites Weekly reflection I learned that connectivity depends on several layers: addressing, routing, network access controls and service configuration. A network diagram helps investigate each layer rather than changing multiple settings at once.
Point to clarify Placing a resource in a public subnet does not by itself ensure Internet reachability. Public addressing, routes and access rules must also be considered.

title: IAM, VPC and secure connectivity
content:
1. Select the account and network Identify the account/Region and add Project=CloudDocs and Environment=demo tags to supported resources. Use an appropriate existing VPC or create a lab VPC: EC2 needs a subnet with suitable outbound connectivity; RDS needs a DB subnet group covering subnets in at least two Availability Zones. A Single-AZ RDS instance still requires a valid subnet group.
2. Security groups Group Intended inbound access Notes clouddocs-web-sg Port 443 from users; port 80 for redirects/certificate issuance if needed Nginx terminates TLS; do not expose port 8080 clouddocs-db-sg Port 3306 from clouddocs-web-sg Do not expose MySQL to the entire Internet Administration Session Manager with the required permissions/connectivity; IP-restricted SSH if needed Session Manager does not work without its prerequisites A private RDS instance cannot be reached directly from a laptop over the Internet. Use an authorized administrative path such as a tunnel, SSM, VPN or operations from EC2; do not make it public simply to bypass a network error.
3. EC2 IAM role Create a role trusted by EC2 and attach a policy scoped to the project’s bucket/prefix. Replace ACCOUNT/BUCKET for the deployment environment before applying the example:
{ "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ {"Effect":"Allow","Action":"s3:ListBucket","Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_BUCKET","Condition":{"StringLike":{"s3:prefix":["documents","documents/*"]}}}, {"Effect":"Allow","Action":["s3:GetObject","s3:PutObject","s3:DeleteObject"],"Resource":"arn:aws:s3:::YOUR_BUCKET/documents/*"} ] } Attach the role using an instance profile; the backend uses the default credential provider chain. HeadObject requires GetObject permission. SSE-KMS requires appropriate KMS permissions and key policy. Do not send AWS access keys to the frontend.
4. Cross-account access, if applicable Configure this only for the actual deployment accounts. AssumeRole requires the trust policy, sts:AssumeRole permission and matching credential flow; a policy on only one side is insufficient. Direct resource-policy access requires checking both the role and bucket policies. This is an environment-dependent deployment option, not an assumed existing configuration.
Verification: EC2 reaches RDS through the correct security groups; the backend has Get/Put/Delete access to the project prefix; public origins cannot access database/backend ports.
Practice and illustrated results T02. EC2 IAM role Open EC2 → Instances → select the instance → Security to inspect the IAM role and security groups. The screenshot records CloudDocsEc2Role attached to the administration bridge instance.
T03. EC2 security group inbound rules Open the security group → Inbound rules. The pictured clouddocs-ssm-ec2-sg allows HTTP on port 80 from 0.0.0.0/0. This records a demo configuration; it does not demonstrate HTTPS or a review of every group attached to the instance.
T04. S3 access policy contents In IAM, inspect the policy allowing GetObject, PutObject and DeleteObject on clouddocs-dev-private/documents/*. The screenshot shows the policy editor and documents the intended permissions; verify that the saved policy is attached to the role when validating access.
T05. Role trust relationship Open IAM → Roles → CloudDocsEc2Role → Trust relationships. The ec2.amazonaws.com principal and sts:AssumeRole allow EC2 to assume the role; S3 operations are separately governed by permission and bucket policies.

title: Private S3 and CORS configuration
content:
1. Create or verify the bucket In the S3 Console, select the project bucket in the agreed Region. Keep Block Public Access, Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership and default encryption enabled. Review existing data before changing an active bucket. Do not enable public website hosting for the document bucket.
The backend uses the documents/ prefix and UUID keys. Policy, CORS and script examples are in Back_end/aws/s3. Running these tools changes infrastructure; they are not mandatory application startup steps.
2. Configure CORS for the actual origin Example for S3 Console → Permissions → CORS; replace the origin:
[ { "AllowedHeaders": ["*"], "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "HEAD"], "AllowedOrigins": ["https://YOUR_FRONTEND_HOST"], "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"], "MaxAgeSeconds": 3600 } ] The Console expects the array of rules shown above. AWS CLI JSON wraps rules in a CORSRules object, as in the repository example. For local development, add the exact active origin, such as http://localhost:5500 or http://127.0.0.1:5500. CORS does not replace IAM or make a bucket public.
The current upload flow passes through the backend and does not depend on S3 CORS; direct preview/download still requires appropriate CORS. Backend PutObject permission comes from IAM/bucket policies. The older practice configuration in H04 also allows PUT; this is not required for the current upload flow.
3. Backend configuration Variable Required value AWS_REGION Actual bucket Region S3_BUCKET The project’s bucket name S3_PRESIGN_EXPIRY Lifetime in seconds; current default is 900 and may be reduced as required 4. Test the normal workflow Sign in and select a file with an optional description; the destination folder belongs to the current account. The frontend sends POST /api/documents/upload as multipart with file, metadata, requestId (UUID) and optional folderId. Use the current UI/DTO rather than guessing JSON fields. The backend checks permissions/quota, uploads using a separate object key and performs HEAD; metadata is committed only after all processing succeeds. After a lost response, retry the same requestId and file to retrieve the saved document; transaction failure rolls back data and attempts object cleanup. Inspect logs if cleanup fails. Obtain preview-url/download-url using an authorized account and open the new presigned GET URL. The legacy standalone metadata creation and upload-url APIs are blocked; do not follow the former direct browser PUT instructions. Expected result: the private object exists, metadata confirms the upload and unshared accounts are denied access. Previously signed URLs may remain usable until expiration; temporary credential expiration can invalidate them earlier.
Common errors For preview/download 403 errors, check the signing principal, policy, prefix, Region and URL expiration. For CORS, compare the complete scheme/host/port origin and test in a browser. For upload failures, inspect backend logs, PutObject/GetObject permissions and S3 connectivity. For HTTP 413, compare backend/Nginx multipart limits. Do not delete old failed records before checking their corresponding S3 objects.
See CORS and presigned URLs.
Practice and illustrated results H01. Bucket and Region Open S3 → Buckets. The clouddocs-dev-private bucket is in Asia Pacific (Singapore), ap-southeast-1; configure the backend S3 client for this Region.
H02. Block public access Under Permissions, Block all public access is On and Object Ownership is Bucket owner enforced. Documents use authorized access rather than a public bucket website.
H03. Cross-account bucket policy The bucket policy allows CloudDocsEc2Role in account 861358180788 to read, write and delete objects under documents/*. Compare the role ARN with T02/T05 and its permission policy. This is resource-policy access, not evidence that the application assumes a separate S3 role.
H04. Saved CORS configuration Under Permissions → CORS, the saved configuration allows GET, PUT and HEAD from http://54.255.190.1; ExposeHeaders contains ETag and Content-Disposition, and MaxAgeSeconds is 300. This is the origin recorded at capture time; synchronize it when the frontend host or port changes.
H05. Default SSE-S3 encryption Open Properties → Default encryption. The encryption type is SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys; this is not an SSE-KMS configuration.

title: RDS MySQL, schema and migrations
content:
1. Prepare RDS Create or verify a MySQL instance compatible with the application in the RDS Console. Select the prepared VPC/subnet group and database security group; configure storage, backup retention and password management for the environment. Describe a Single-AZ lab accurately rather than calling it Multi-AZ. Record the endpoint, port and schema name in configuration management.
2. Import the base schema The repository does not include a complete empty-database installer. Use a verified schema export, check for sensitive data and import into a test database first. Base business tables such as users/documents/audit_logs must exist. Do not apply incremental migrations to an empty database or enable ddl-auto=update merely to bypass validation failures.
3. Review migrations Order File in Back_end/db/migration Purpose 0 00_PRECHECK.sql Check legacy owner references 1 01_APPLY_document_permissions.sql owner_id and sharing permissions 2 02_APPLY_document_favorites.sql Favorites 3 03_APPLY_notifications.sql Global announcements 4 04_APPLY_cognito_identities.sql issuer/sub identity mapping 5 05_APPLY_optional_contact_email.sql Optional contact email 6 06_APPLY_work_tasks.sql Work tasks and recipient notifications; part of the November update 7 07_APPLY_departments_avatars.sql Departments and avatars 8 08_APPLY_document_folders.sql Document folder hierarchy; existing files remain at the root Apply only missing steps after backing up and preflighting the correct database. Migration 04 and share-cognito-identities.sql are alternative ways to create the same table; do not run them consecutively. MySQL DDL may commit automatically, so ROLLBACK does not undo every ALTER/CREATE.
Migration 08 is required for folders and differs from the optional audit cleanup script in Back_end/db. MANAGER, Sent shares and content replacement require no new migration after 07; folders still require 08.
4. Connect the application Set DB_HOST, DB_PORT, DB_NAME, DB_USERNAME and DB_PASSWORD outside source code. Give the application user only required privileges and keep it separate from the migration administrator.
TLS: the current application.yml contains a local JDBC URL with useSSL=false. For AWS, override SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL with an RDS JDBC URL using sslMode=VERIFY_IDENTITY and configure the correct RDS CA bundle/JVM truststore. Verify the SSL session; changing DB_HOST alone does not establish encryption.
5. Verification Start the backend with the verified schema and confirm that ddl-auto=validate reports no missing tables/columns. Perform authorized test reads/writes, check metadata/audit and capture results with sensitive information hidden. Test backup restoration on a separate database before claiming recovery has been verified.
Practice and illustrated results T07. RDS MySQL overview Open RDS → Databases → clouddocs-mysql → Configuration. The screenshot shows Available status, MySQL Community, the db.t4g.micro class and the company_documents database. Compare these settings with the backend datasource configuration.
T08. RDS endpoint and networking In Connectivity & security, record the endpoint, port 3306, VPC, subnets and security groups. Publicly accessible is Yes in the screenshot, so this does not demonstrate the recommended private RDS setup described above. Actual reachability also depends on networking rules and routes.
T09. Database security group MySQL rule Open rds-ec2-1 → Inbound rules. The pictured rule accepts MySQL/Aurora TCP 3306 from an EC2 security group. Review the other groups attached to the database as well; one group screenshot does not describe all effective network permissions.
T10. RDS connection and data query In the MySQL client, inspect the connection to the RDS endpoint and the company_documents database. SHOW TABLES lists business tables including users, documents, document_permissions, audit_logs and work_tasks. SELECT id, title, file_type, file_size, created_at FROM documents WHERE id IN (35, 36, 37) ORDER BY id returns three document records, illustrating metadata reads from the database. These are the pictured test records and are not assumed to be the same file as H07. The connection information shows SSL: Not in use, so the screenshot demonstrates connectivity and querying, not the TLS configuration recommended above.

title: Cognito and user authentication
content:
1. User Pool and public app client Create or verify the User Pool, domain and web app client. Use a public client without a client secret, Authorization Code grant and PKCE. Callback/logout settings must exactly match actual URLs; use HTTPS for deployment. Select scopes appropriate to UserInfo, usually openid, profile and email according to the application. Do not enable unnecessary grants.
2. Consistent configuration Location Configuration FrontEnd/js/cognito-config.js Domain, client ID, redirectUri/logoutUri and scopes using the actual file structure Backend COGNITO_ISSUER_URI Issuer https://cognito-idp.REGION.amazonaws.com/POOL_ID Backend COGNITO_CLIENT_ID Corresponding public app client ID Backend COGNITO_USER_INFO_URI UserInfo domain for the actual pool Backend CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS Actual frontend origin Do not copy the development issuer/client into another pool’s configuration. Read the values assigned by local scripts rather than assuming externally supplied environment variables remain unchanged.
3. Backend validation and internal identities The backend validates the JWT signature, issuer, validity period, token_use=access, client_id and sub. The system maps issuer/sub to a MySQL account and reads its current role/status. Email and full name are profile data, not substitutes for the identity key.
New accounts receive USER. Review Back_end/db/bootstrap-cognito-admin.sql to bootstrap the first ADMIN; do not arbitrarily edit shared database data. The template defaults to NULL targets/ROLLBACK so the operator can inspect it first.
ADMIN/MANAGER/USER roles are managed by the application in MySQL, not inferred from Cognito status. MANAGER requires an assigned department; department preview follows the owner’s current department and does not automatically grant download/edit/share/delete permissions.
4. Testing Test sign-in, callback, GET /api/auth/me and logout. Missing, invalid or expired tokens must be rejected; USER must not call administrative APIs; locked/DELETED accounts must be denied business access. Logout does not instantly invalidate every access-token copy; document the actual behavior accurately.
See Cognito PKCE.
Practice and illustrated results S01. User Pool overview Open Cognito → User pools → the application pool. Compare the Pool ID and us-east-1 Region when configuring the issuer; this Region differs from S3/RDS.
S02. Frontend app client Choose App clients → clouddocs-web. Client secret is shown as a dash, consistent with a client without a secret. The React selection in the Console quick-start guide does not establish the actual frontend technology used by the project.
S03–S04. Callback, logout, grant and scopes In Login pages, inspect callback/logout URLs, the Authorization code grant and email, openid and profile scopes. The screenshot records localhost/127.0.0.1 URLs for local use; deployment requires registering the actual frontend URLs. A grant configuration screenshot alone does not prove that the browser performed PKCE.
S05. Sign-in domain Open Branding → Domain and use the pool domain to synchronize the application authorize, token, UserInfo and logout configuration.
S06. Cognito test users Open Users to inspect accounts, Email verified, Confirmation status and Enabled status. CloudDocs ADMIN/MANAGER/USER roles are managed in application data and cannot be inferred from Cognito Confirmed status.

title: Feedback and suggestions
content:
My name is Lê Hoàng Tùng, a student in class K68CNTTA at Vietnam National University of Agriculture, participating in the First Cloud AI Journey program. During the internship, I studied AWS services and was responsible for the EC2 and RDS components of CloudDocs. This helped me connect what I had learned with deploying and operating a practical application.
Assessment by aspect 1. Internship environment
The program enabled me to study independently using Cloud Journey materials and relate concepts to project work. A topic-based learning path gave me clearer direction while helping me develop independent research habits and organize my study time.
2. Mentorship and support
Documentation and community discussions gave me additional ways to approach unfamiliar topics. I found that preparing configuration details, error messages and attempted steps made discussions more effective.

The internship topics connected with networking, databases and web development studied at university. Participating in a project helped me understand how these concepts work together in a system and recognize the importance of communication and coordination between team members.

Better understanding of the roles of EC2 and RDS in the CloudDocs architecture. Practice in checking server configurations, database connection details and network access permissions. Coordinating with team members to compare infrastructure and application configurations. 5. Community culture
Shared materials and meetup activities exposed me to further learning and working experiences with AWS. I found the community a suitable place for newcomers to ask questions, discuss difficulties and learn from more experienced members.
6. Internship conditions
Online resources gave me flexibility to study and look up information as needed. Effective learning required setting aside time for practice, recording results and discussing difficulties. Using AWS resources also helped me become more aware of cost tracking and learning-environment management.
Feedback questions and suggestions What satisfied me most?
I was most satisfied with the opportunity to connect what I had learned with a concrete project rather than studying each topic in isolation. Participating in CloudDocs helped me develop responsibility, coordinate with the team and recognize skills I need to improve.
What could the program improve?
Add step-by-step exercises with expected outcomes and common errors so newcomers can check their work. Offer more discussions with mentors about challenging topics and approaches to difficulties. Explain how to maintain a worklog, select useful resources and collect evidence from the beginning of the internship. Would I recommend the program to friends?
Yes. I would recommend it to friends who want to learn AWS and are willing to take an active role in learning. Combining documentation with a concrete project helps learners connect concepts with practical work.
Additional suggestions Organize short exchanges between learners to share study and teamwork experiences. Add career-orientation discussions to help students understand Cloud roles and the skills they require. Provide general guidance on cost management, handover and resource cleanup at the end of exercises or projects. Would I like to stay involved with the program?
Yes. I would like to continue learning through Cloud Journey, participate in suitable community activities and apply my knowledge to further exercises and projects. I also hope to share the experience I gain so that other learners and I can progress together.
Acknowledgments
I thank the mentors and the First Cloud AI Journey community for sharing their knowledge and experience during the internship. Learning and participating in CloudDocs helped me clarify my direction and recognize the skills I need to keep developing.

title: EC2, Nginx and operations
content:
1. Prepare the server Create or verify an appropriate Linux EC2 instance, S3 instance profile and network security group. Install Java 21 and Nginx using packages appropriate to the OS. Build the JAR in a verified environment and transfer it and FrontEnd to the server. The current frontend needs neither npm install nor npm build. Do not serve the entire repository through the web server.
2. Backend environment configuration Keep configuration in an environment file readable only by the operator, outside the web root and repository. Minimum variables:
Variable Purpose SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=aws Deployment profile DB_HOST / DB_PORT / DB_NAME / DB_USERNAME / DB_PASSWORD Database connection SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL TLS JDBC override described in the RDS section AWS_REGION / S3_BUCKET / S3_PRESIGN_EXPIRY Environment-specific S3 settings COGNITO_ISSUER_URI / COGNITO_CLIENT_ID / COGNITO_USER_INFO_URI Authentication against the correct pool CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS Frontend origin PORT=8080 Backend accessed only through the reverse proxy Replace paths and the actual JAR in this systemd example. Create the clouddocs system user first and grant it access to configuration and application files. An example JAR name is not a command that can be used unchanged in every environment.
[Unit] Description=CloudDocs backend After=network-online.target Wants=network-online.target [Service] User=clouddocs WorkingDirectory=/opt/clouddocs EnvironmentFile=/etc/clouddocs/backend.env ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /opt/clouddocs/backend.jar Restart=on-failure RestartSec=5 SuccessExitStatus=143 [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target Rename the tested deployment build to backend.jar and verify that /usr/bin/java is Java 21. Run systemctl daemon-reload and enable/start according to the administration procedure, then inspect journalctl -u clouddocs for errors. Keep passwords/tokens out of logs.
3. Serve the frontend and proxy with Nginx Example inside an HTTPS server with a valid certificate; replace the domain, certificate and directories for the actual server:
root /var/www/clouddocs; index index.html; client_max_body_size 101m; location / { try_files $uri $uri/ =404; } location /api/ { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; } Upload and replacement pass through the backend. The Nginx limit of 101 MiB accommodates a 100 MiB file plus multipart overhead; align the Spring Boot limits. Test uploads through the actual deployment origin to detect HTTP 413 and timeout issues before acceptance.
Copy the contents of FrontEnd into the web root in this example. If the callback uses /FrontEnd/, preserve that prefix in directory/Nginx configuration; changing Cognito alone is insufficient. Set API_BASE for the actual hostname/backend. Run nginx -t before reloading. Redirect port 80 to HTTPS according to environment policy; a domain/certificate is a prerequisite rather than an assumed existing resource.
4. Monitoring, backups and costs Basic EC2 CloudWatch monitoring includes CPU, network and status checks. RAM, filesystem and application logs require the agent, permissions and suitable networking. Set retention, generate a controlled error and verify that its log arrives. Configure RDS backup/snapshot retention and test restoration on a copy. Set a budget with the appropriate account, recipient and threshold; Budgets is not a switch that automatically stops every resource.
Secrets Manager may be added later, but the application currently reads environment variables. Creating a secret does not automatically make Spring Boot retrieve it.
5. Deployment evidence Record the EC2 instance, commit/JAR, deployment time, HTTPS URL, /api/health, RDS connection, S3 upload and Cognito sign-in. Use endpoints, hostnames and screenshots from the actual CloudDocs environment under test.
Practice and illustrated results T01. EC2 in the practice environment EC2 → Instances records clouddocs-ssm-bridge-1b as Running, with a t3.micro type and passed status checks. Its private DNS ip-172-31-16-134 matches the hostname in T06; the terminal check below adds evidence of the backend service running on this instance at capture time.
T06. Running backend and health check In the EC2 terminal session, run hostname and date -Is to record the host and verification time. systemctl is-active clouddocs returns active; curl to http://127.0.0.1:8080/actuator/health returns {“status”:“UP”} and HTTP 200. Hostname ip-172-31-16-134 matches the private DNS in T01, providing evidence that the backend was running on this instance at capture time. The pictured endpoint is /actuator/health; this result does not replace sign-in, file transfer or external access tests.

title: Business and integration testing
content:
Test prerequisites Prepare at least one ADMIN, one MANAGER with an assigned department and two active USER accounts linked to Cognito; arrange accounts in the same/different departments, an authorized small file, an empty file and an oversized file for rejection tests. Use test data and record the commit, environment, tester and time. The following table lists scenarios and expected results, not preassigned passing outcomes.
ID Scenario Expected result AUTH-01 Missing, invalid or expired access token Business API rejects the request without exposing content AUTH-02 USER calls an administrative API Access denied DOC-01 Send multipart to POST /api/documents/upload Backend stores/confirms S3 before commit; metadata is correct and readable DOC-02 Concurrent uploads with identical filenames Distinct object keys; no unintended overwrite DOC-03 S3 upload/confirmation fails within the transaction Metadata rolls back; attempt cleanup of the upload object and log cleanup failures DOC-04 Zero-byte file Preview/download handles the file appropriately for its format DOC-05 File exceeds 100 MiB or the account quota Rejected; allocations remain within the quota DOC-06 Lose the response after successful upload; retry the same requestId/file Return the saved document without creating a duplicate DOC-07 Replace a file with EDIT permission and no report protection Preserve ID/owner/shares/favorites; update content and size ACL-01 Grant VIEW to USER B B can preview but cannot obtain download/edit access ACL-02 Grant DOWNLOAD/EDIT Only the corresponding actions are allowed; sharing administration is not implied ACL-03 USER C has no share API denies preview/download/edit ACL-04 Revoke B’s permission New URL requests are blocked; previously issued URLs may remain valid until expiration ACL-05 MANAGER accesses documents owned by accounts in the same/different department Additional preview only within the department; no automatic download/edit/share/delete permission ACL-06 Change/revoke one or multiple permissions in Sent shares Only owner/ADMIN manages shares; new permissions apply on subsequent API requests FOLDER-01 Create subfolders and move one/multiple owned files Correct hierarchy; preserve S3 keys, shares and favorites FOLDER-02 USER/MANAGER organizes another account’s files or folders Denied even when document preview is allowed FOLDER-03 Delete a folder tree containing a protected report Cancel the whole operation; no partial move to trash TRASH-01 Owner moves a file to trash Preview/download/edit/share are blocked; quota still includes the file TRASH-02 Restore a file Returns to ACTIVE and preserves earlier shares as designed TRASH-03 Permanently delete a test file Object/permissions removed; metadata becomes PURGED with size 0; audit retained BULK-01 Select multiple files including one permission failure Show individual success/failure and allow retrying failed items QUOTA-01 Successful/failed uploads, trash and shared documents Rolled-back uploads do not increase committed usage; trash counts against the owner; sharing does not multiply allocation AUDIT-01 USER/ADMIN reads audit records USER sees their own actor events; ADMIN sees system-wide events TASK-01 ADMIN assigns work; USER submits a valid document Private notification and SUBMITTED/pending approval status TASK-02 Creator requests changes, then approves Only authorized actor proceeds; feedback, audit and notifications recorded TASK-03 Submit after the deadline Submission accepted and labeled late; reviewer delay does not make a pending approval overdue TASK-04 Two tabs use an outdated version HTTP 409; user must reload current data TASK-05 Delete/overwrite a SUBMITTED/COMPLETED report file API blocks the operation using the current release’s guard TASK-06 Delete one or multiple tasks Only the assigning ADMIN/MANAGER; retain documents/permissions/audit and handle related notifications TASK-07 MANAGER assigns work within/across departments Only active USER accounts in the same department; no assignment to another MANAGER USER-01 Delete an account with files or unfinished tasks Blocked according to current conditions DEPT-01 USER/MANAGER calls department management or role-change APIs Denied; ADMIN manages data subject to constraints UI-01 Search/filter/sort and select all with more than 20 items Browser-side pagination; select only eligible rows on the current page Actual results and evidence scope The table below summarizes what the stored evidence demonstrates and what still requires verification. Screenshots record individual moments and do not establish a shared commit or show that every scenario above passed. According to Tran Hai Luong’s reference report, current-release descriptions were checked against the CloudDocs source on 16 November 2026; this evidence set contains no test-suite execution results tied to an acceptance commit/JAR.

Tests using mock repositories/AWS clients do not verify live RDS migrations, row locking, Cognito redirects, S3 CORS or browser PDF rendering. Record results for each test execution.

Rows show recipients, the Nhân sự department, sharing times and View or Edit access; each row includes a permission selector and Revoke button. Multiple grants can also be selected for revocation. No replacement file is selected and no save confirmation is shown, so the screenshot records the editing interface before submission.

Account information shows ADMIN and Active status. Interface guidance accepts JPG/PNG up to 5 MB with a centered square crop. The screenshot illustrates an existing profile and update controls; no before/after pair or save confirmation is provided.

The screenshot records 4 tasks, 1 Pending approval and 0 Overdue; individual rows show Not started, In progress, Pending approval and Completed. title: Week 9: Studying Amazon CloudWatch and system monitoring
content:
Period: 05/10/2026 – 09/10/2026.
After studying application components, I consider how to recognize normal operation. CloudWatch is examined through metrics, logs, alarms and correlating failure signals.
Weekly objectives Distinguish metrics, logs, dashboards and alarms. Identify monitoring information relevant to EC2, RDS and the CloudDocs backend. Learning activities Day Study and review activity Start date Completion date Study sources Monday Study metrics, namespaces and dimensions. Review EC2 CPU and RDS database-connection examples. 05/10/2026 05/10/2026 Viewing CloudWatch metrics

Distinguish default EC2 metrics from operating-system metrics such as memory that require additional collection. 07/10/2026 07/10/2026 Install CloudWatch Agent to collect operating-system metrics Thursday Review alarm thresholds, evaluation periods and missing-data handling. Study notifications through Amazon SNS. 08/10/2026 08/10/2026 Create CloudWatch alarms and notifications Friday Outline a slow-backend investigation: correlate error timing, CPU, database connections and application logs. 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 Viewing CloudWatch metrics
CloudWatch Logs, log groups and log streams Weekly reflection I learned that one metric rarely establishes the cause of a failure. Metrics should be correlated with logs over the same time window, with thresholds chosen for the application.
Point to clarify Passwords, access tokens and presigned URLs should not be logged. Log retention and collection levels also affect monitoring costs.

title: Cleanup and handover
content:
Before cleanup Clean up only authorized demo resources. Check whether resources are still needed for the project through 28 November; do not remove shared infrastructure at the end of an individual workshop session. Inventory resource IDs, Regions/accounts, ownership and data to retain. This guide does not execute AWS resource deletions.
Handover Keep the commit/JAR and startup instructions, a secret-free configuration inventory, applied schema/migrations, test results and evidence. Store backups only in approved locations and test restoration on a copy. Signed URLs and access tokens are not handover materials.
Demo cleanup sequence after confirmation Stop application access/processes and record configuration that must be retained. Back up the database if needed, then remove the designated demo RDS instance; check final snapshots and retained backups for continuing charges. Handle identified S3 test files. If Versioning is enabled, review versions and delete markers separately; deleting the current object does not delete every version. Terminate demo EC2 instances when no longer needed; check retained EBS, snapshots and public IPv4/Elastic IPs. Delete demo Cognito pools/clients only when no longer used; retain any pool still used by the project. Review CloudWatch log groups/alarms, networking such as NAT/endpoints, IAM roles/policies and other resources actually created. Check Billing across Regions after updates propagate. Stopping EC2 does not eliminate charges for retained EBS, snapshots or allocated IPs. Expected result: a handover record and retained/deleted resource inventory. Do not claim zero costs before reconciling the bill.

content:

This week expands from one server to multiple serving components. I study traffic distribution, instance-count adjustment and reducing dependence on one deployment location.
Weekly objectives Distinguish load balancing, scaling and availability. Analyze prerequisites for running the CloudDocs backend across multiple servers. Identify limitations of increasing the size of a single EC2 instance. 19/10/2026 19/10/2026 Create an Auto Scaling group and scaling policy Tuesday Study Application Load Balancers, listeners, target groups and health checks. Create a target group and configure health checks Wednesday Review launch templates, Auto Scaling groups and minimum, desired and maximum capacities. Study metric-based scaling policies. 21/10/2026 21/10/2026 Create a launch template
Create an Auto Scaling group and scaling policy Thursday Study placement across Availability Zones. Distinguish application-tier availability from database-tier availability. 22/10/2026 22/10/2026 WordPress architecture with Auto Scaling, a load balancer and RDS
Create RDS MySQL and configure Multi-AZ Friday Sketch a possible CloudDocs scaling design. Review sessions, local files, shared configuration and database connections across backends. 23/10/2026 23/10/2026 WordPress architecture with Auto Scaling, a load balancer and RDS Weekly reflection I learned that adding servers alone does not establish high availability. Health checks, shared data and remaining failure points must also be considered. The multi-AZ architecture here is an analysis, not a confirmed deployment outcome.
Point to clarify Auto Scaling does not resolve every performance bottleneck. Adding backends may not help when database capacity or state management is the limiting factor.
